Finance and fintech

What is a merchant account? Where does your customer's money actually go?

Published by Stackwire. Published 13 November 2026.

A merchant account is a payment account used by an acquiring bank or payment provider to receive and manage funds from card transactions before they are paid out to a business. It is one part of the card-payment system, not simply another name for the business's everyday bank account.

Quick answer

When a customer pays by card, the payment is first authorized. After the business captures the payment, the transaction is cleared and settled through the card network and financial institutions. In a traditional acquiring setup, the acquirer credits the merchant account, then pays out the available balance to the business's nominated bank account according to the agreement. With an all-in-one payment facilitator, the business may instead use a sub-account or balance within the provider's platform rather than opening its own dedicated merchant account.

What is a merchant account?

A merchant account is an account arrangement that allows a business to accept card payments. In a traditional model, it is provided through an acquiring bank or an acquirer working with a payment processor. It receives the proceeds of card transactions after settlement, subject to processing fees, refunds, disputes, reserves and the terms of the merchant agreement.

It is not normally the account a business uses for rent, payroll and everyday banking. The merchant account sits within the payment-acceptance arrangement. The business's regular bank account is where the provider ultimately sends payouts.

The word merchant simply means the business accepting the payment. A shop, subscription company, hotel or online retailer can all be merchants. The account structure behind their payments may look different depending on whether they work directly with an acquirer or use a payment facilitator.

Merchant account vs business bank account

Merchant accountBusiness bank account
Part of the card-acceptance and acquiring arrangement.The business's everyday deposit account with a bank or financial institution.
Receives or records card-payment proceeds during settlement, depending on the provider model.Receives payouts and is used for normal business banking.
Subject to payment-processing terms, fees, reserves, refunds and dispute rules.Subject to the bank account agreement and applicable banking rules.
May be a dedicated merchant account or a provider-managed sub-account arrangement.Usually held in the business's name, subject to the bank's onboarding requirements.

Some payment platforms make the distinction less visible because they show a single balance and payout dashboard. That interface does not necessarily mean the underlying funds are held in a traditional merchant account in the business's own name. Ask the provider how the arrangement works legally and operationally.

How does a merchant account work?

The key is to separate authorization from settlement. An approval at checkout does not mean the money has already reached the business's bank account.

  1. The customer pays. They enter card details or use a digital wallet at checkout.
  2. The payment request is authorized. The gateway or payment platform securely sends the transaction into the processing chain. The acquirer and card network route the request to the customer's issuing bank, which approves or declines it.
  3. The business captures the payment. Depending on the setup, capture may happen immediately or later. For example, a retailer may authorize a card when an order is placed and capture the amount when the goods ship.
  4. The transaction is cleared and settled. Transaction information is exchanged and funds move through the relevant institutions. In a traditional acquiring model, the acquirer credits the merchant account, subject to fees and other adjustments.
  5. The provider pays out the balance. The available funds are transferred to the business's nominated bank account according to the payout schedule and any applicable holds or reserves.

Visa explains that an acquiring bank can hold settled funds in a merchant account, while a payment facilitator may operate under a shared acquiring account rather than requiring every seller to establish its own. The exact flow can vary by provider, country, card scheme and payment method.

Who is involved in a card payment?

  • Customer / cardholder: the person making the purchase.
  • Issuing bank: the financial institution that issued the customer's card. It makes the authorization decision.
  • Merchant: the business selling the product or service.
  • Acquirer / acquiring bank: the merchant's acquiring-side institution. It connects the business to the card-payment system and handles settlement under the acquiring arrangement.
  • Payment processor: the technology and services that route transaction messages and support processing between the parties.
  • Payment gateway: the checkout-facing technology that securely captures or transmits payment details. It may be supplied separately or bundled with other services.
  • Card network: the network, such as Visa or Mastercard, that carries messages and coordinates rules and settlement between participants.

One provider may perform several of these functions. That is why it is important to compare what a company actually supplies rather than assuming every provider uses the same labels. For a deeper explanation, see our guide to payment gateways vs payment processors.

Dedicated merchant account vs payment facilitator

Not every business opens a separate merchant account directly with an acquiring bank. Many small businesses sign up with a payment facilitator (often called a PayFac) or an all-in-one payment service provider. The platform onboards the business and enables it to accept payments under the provider's acquiring arrangement.

Dedicated merchant accountPayment facilitator / aggregated model
The business is typically underwritten for its own merchant account with an acquirer.The platform onboards the business as a sub-merchant or connected account under its broader arrangement.
May provide more direct control over acquiring terms and a tailored setup.Often offers faster onboarding and a bundled checkout, processing and reporting experience.
Can involve more underwriting, documentation, negotiation and provider management.Provider controls eligibility, account limits, reserves, payout rules and supported business types under its terms.
May suit established businesses with stable volume, specific needs or more complex payment operations.May suit smaller businesses that value simpler setup and an integrated service.

Visa explains that payment facilitators can enable smaller businesses to accept payments through a shared acquiring arrangement instead of each business setting up its own merchant account. The exact legal structure and terminology differ by market and provider. A platform balance or connected account should not automatically be described as a separate bank account owned by the seller.

What fees can a merchant account involve?

There is no single universal merchant-account fee. The total cost depends on the provider, business type, card mix, country, transaction volume, risk profile and negotiated terms. Common charges can include:

  • Interchange: a fee associated with the card transaction and paid within the card system to the card issuer. Rates vary by card type, region and transaction category.
  • Card-network assessments: network-related charges that may be included in a provider's pricing breakdown.
  • Processor or acquirer markup: the provider's charge for processing, acquiring and related services.
  • Gateway or platform fees: charges for checkout technology, integrations or platform features, where applicable.
  • Fixed transaction fees: a set amount charged on each successful payment.
  • Other costs: monthly minimums, cross-border fees, currency conversion, chargebacks, retrieval requests, hardware, PCI-related services or early termination charges, depending on the agreement.

Some providers bundle several costs into one flat rate. Others use interchange-plus or custom pricing. A headline percentage is not enough to compare offers; review the full fee schedule and model it against your actual payment mix. Our guide to choosing a payment processor explains flat-rate and interchange-plus pricing in more detail.

Worked example: what might card processing cost?

Here is a simple illustration using Stripe's published US standard online domestic-card rate at the time of writing: 2.9% + $0.30 per successful transaction. This is a provider-specific example, not a universal merchant-account price.

Example: 100 payments of $100 each
  • Total sales: 100 × $100 = $10,000
  • Percentage fees: 2.9% × $10,000 = $290
  • Fixed fees: 100 × $0.30 = $30
  • Total example processing fees: $320
  • Amount remaining after these fees: $9,680

This illustration assumes every payment qualifies for the stated standard domestic online-card rate. It excludes any other products or services, taxes, refunds, disputes, international-card surcharges and currency conversion. Stripe's pricing can differ by country, payment method and account arrangement, so check the current pricing page and your own agreement before budgeting.

Why can payouts be delayed or held?

A successful checkout does not guarantee an immediate bank deposit. The provider may need to complete settlement, apply its payout schedule, verify account information or review unusual activity. A business may also be subject to a reserve or temporary hold under its agreement.

Common reasons include:

  • Normal settlement and payout timing: processing and bank-transfer schedules take time and vary by country and provider.
  • New-account review: providers may review a new merchant's business model, identity, website or expected transaction pattern.
  • Unusual activity: a sudden increase in sales, unusually large transactions or a change in customer or geographic mix may trigger a review.
  • Refunds and disputes: the provider may retain funds to cover expected refunds, chargebacks or other liabilities, where its agreement and applicable rules allow.
  • Incomplete verification: missing business, beneficial-owner or bank details can delay onboarding or payouts.

Before relying on a provider for cash flow, read its payout schedule, reserve policy, account-review process and dispute terms. Ask what happens if the account is paused and how you can contact support.

How should a business choose a merchant account provider?

Start with the countries where you are legally able to operate and the payment methods your customers use. Then compare providers on the full service, not just the advertised rate.

  1. Confirm eligibility. Check supported countries, business types, restricted activities, required documents and settlement currencies.
  2. Compare the full price. Ask for percentage and fixed fees, interchange treatment, monthly charges, cross-border and conversion costs, dispute fees and any minimums.
  3. Understand the account model. Ask whether you receive a dedicated merchant account or operate as a sub-merchant / connected account under a payment facilitator.
  4. Check payout and reserve terms. Confirm standard payout timing, weekend and holiday treatment, reserve rights, hold triggers and how funds are released.
  5. Review risk and dispute support. Understand fraud tools, chargeback notifications, evidence submission, refund workflows and who is responsible at each stage.
  6. Test the integration. Review checkout options, APIs, plugins, reporting, reconciliation exports, webhooks and customer support.
  7. Read the contract. Check termination rights, rolling reserves, account closure, data portability, price changes and dispute procedures before signing.

For a small business with straightforward needs, an integrated payment provider may be the simplest place to start. A larger or more complex merchant may benefit from a dedicated acquiring relationship and negotiated pricing. Neither model is automatically cheaper or safer; the right fit depends on the business.

Common merchant account misconceptions

  • “A merchant account is my business bank account.” No. It is part of the card-acceptance arrangement; payouts generally go to a nominated bank account.
  • “Every business needs its own dedicated merchant account.” No. A payment facilitator can onboard businesses under a shared acquiring arrangement.
  • “An approved payment means the money is in my bank.” No. Authorization, capture, clearing, settlement and payout are distinct steps.
  • “The lowest advertised rate is always the cheapest.” Not necessarily. Fixed fees, card mix, international payments, reserves and dispute costs affect the real total.
  • “The provider can never hold my money.” Payouts may be delayed or reserves applied under the provider's agreement and applicable rules. Read those terms before signing.

Frequently asked questions

What is a merchant account in simple terms?

It is an account arrangement that lets a business accept card payments. In a traditional setup, the acquirer uses it to receive settled card-payment funds before paying the available balance to the business's bank account.

Do I need a merchant account to accept credit cards?

You need an acquiring or payment-provider arrangement that can process card payments, but you may not need to open a separate merchant account yourself. An all-in-one PSP or payment facilitator may provide access through its platform.

Is a merchant account a bank account?

It is not the same as the business's everyday bank account. A traditional merchant account is part of the acquiring arrangement for card payments. The provider typically pays out funds to the business's nominated bank account.

What is the difference between a merchant account and a payment processor?

The merchant account is the account arrangement used to receive or manage card-payment proceeds during settlement. The processor handles transaction messages and processing between the merchant, acquirer, card networks and banks. A provider may supply both services.

How long does it take to receive money from a merchant account?

There is no universal timeline. It depends on the country, payment method, provider, settlement schedule, bank-transfer timing, account history and any review or reserve. Check the provider's written payout terms.

Can a small business get a merchant account?

Many small businesses can accept card payments through an acquirer or payment facilitator if they meet the provider's eligibility and verification requirements. Available providers and rules differ by country and business type.

Why would a merchant account be frozen or put on hold?

A provider may review unusual transaction activity, suspected fraud, disputes, incomplete verification or potential violations of its terms. The agreement should explain review, reserve and payout procedures. Contact the provider for the specific reason and the steps needed to resolve it.

Bottom line

A merchant account is part of the infrastructure that lets a business accept card payments and receive the proceeds after settlement. The important question is not only whether a provider offers a merchant account, but how its account model works, when it pays out, what it charges and what happens when a transaction is refunded or disputed. Understand those details before choosing a provider.

Sources and further reading

  • Visa Acceptance Solutions: Payments — roles of the issuer, acquirer, processor and payment facilitator, plus a simplified payment flow.
  • Stripe: Payment processor vs. merchant account — additional background on how the services work together.
  • Stripe: US pricing — published standard online domestic-card pricing used for the illustrative fee calculation. Pricing can change; check the live page.
  • Visa: Beyond the Acquirer — Additional Visa Acceptance Entities — background on authorization and settlement.

This article is general educational information, not legal, banking, tax or financial advice. Provider terms, payment rules and availability vary by country and business type. Information checked 13 November 2026.

Finance and fintech

How businesses can receive USDC payments and convert them to dollars

Published by Stackwire. Published 10 November 2026.

A business may want the speed of a stablecoin payment without keeping cryptocurrency on its balance sheet. A new PNC and Coinbase pilot shows one way a bank can receive USDC and convert it into a regular dollar deposit.

Quick answer

Some payment and banking services let eligible businesses receive USDC and convert it into US dollars before the money reaches a bank account. In PNC's limited pilot announced on 9 November 2026, eligible Corporate and Institutional Banking clients can receive USDC on Ethereum through Coinbase Payment products. PNC says incoming payments are automatically converted 1-to-1 into dollars and deposited into a designated PNC account. This is not a service currently available to every business.

What does it mean to accept USDC as a business?

USDC is a digital token designed to maintain a value of one US dollar. It can be transferred on supported blockchain networks. When a business accepts USDC, the payment arrives as a token rather than through the usual card or bank-transfer rails.

That does not automatically mean the business wants to hold crypto. A payment provider or banking partner may convert the incoming token into fiat currency, such as US dollars, and arrange for the funds to be credited to a bank account. The exact process depends on the provider, network, account eligibility and contract.

How the PNC and Coinbase pilot works

On 9 November 2026, PNC Bank announced that eligible clients of its Corporate and Institutional Banking business can receive USDC payments on Ethereum. Coinbase Payment products provide the payment infrastructure. PNC says incoming USDC is automatically converted 1-to-1 into US dollars and deposited into a designated PNC deposit account.

Announced payment flow
  1. A customer sends USDC on Ethereum.
  2. The payment is handled through Coinbase Payment products.
  3. The incoming USDC is converted 1-to-1 into US dollars.
  4. The dollars are deposited into the participating business's designated PNC account.

This describes the PNC pilot announced by the companies. Other providers may use different networks, conversion arrangements and settlement processes.

The companies describe the service as a limited pilot for eligible corporate and institutional clients. The public announcement does not provide a universal sign-up route for small businesses, a complete fee schedule or a guaranteed settlement-time benchmark.

Why might a business consider stablecoin payments?

  • Cross-border collection: a customer and supplier may be able to transfer a supported stablecoin without using the same local payment network.
  • Payment availability: blockchain transfers can operate outside conventional banking hours, although conversion and bank-account crediting may still depend on provider processes.
  • Dollar settlement: automatic conversion can let a participating business receive a dollar deposit instead of managing a USDC balance itself.
  • New customer options: a business serving customers already using digital assets may want another way to collect payment.

These are potential benefits, not a promise that every stablecoin payment will be faster or cheaper than a bank transfer. A business should compare the complete journey from customer payment to usable funds in its account.

What should a business check before accepting USDC?

CheckWhy it mattersQuestion to ask
EligibilitySome services are limited to selected business types, locations or existing bank clients.Can our legal entity and country use this service?
NetworkUSDC exists on more than one supported blockchain. Sending on the wrong network can cause loss or delay.Which network and token contract must the payer use?
ConversionThe conversion rate, timing and provider process affect the amount received.When does conversion happen, and what rate is applied?
FeesNetwork, service, conversion or bank fees may affect the final amount.What is the total cost from payment to bank deposit?
ReconciliationFinance teams need to match the payment to an invoice and customer.What transaction references and reports are provided?
ComplianceBusinesses may have customer, sanctions, tax and recordkeeping obligations.Which checks and records are our responsibility?
Refunds and disputesBlockchain transfers are not the same as card chargebacks.How are mistakes, refunds and disputed payments handled?

USDC payments are not the same as a bank transfer

A bank transfer moves money through banking and payment systems. A USDC payment transfers a token on a blockchain. A provider may connect that blockchain payment to a bank deposit, but the two stages remain different.

That distinction matters when a payment is sent to the wrong address, uses an unsupported network, or needs to be refunded. Blockchain transfers generally do not have the same built-in reversal and chargeback process as card payments. Businesses need clear procedures for verifying payment instructions and resolving mistakes before accepting funds.

Does automatic conversion remove the risks?

No. Conversion can reduce the need for a business to hold a stablecoin, but it does not remove every risk. A business still needs to understand provider and bank eligibility, the network being used, transaction monitoring, operational controls, settlement timing, fees and how exceptions are handled.

USDC is designed to track the US dollar, but it is not the same thing as cash in an insured bank deposit account. Stablecoins also involve issuer, reserve, custody, technology and regulatory considerations. Read the issuer's disclosures and the service provider's terms rather than assuming a one-dollar target guarantees a risk-free payment.

Is this suitable for small businesses?

It depends on the business's customers, countries, payment volume, banking relationships and the service available to it. The PNC announcement is specifically about eligible corporate and institutional clients in a limited pilot. It should not be read as proof that a small business can open an account and start receiving USDC through PNC today.

A smaller business should first compare the payment options it can actually access. If its customers already pay reliably through bank transfers or card payments, a new stablecoin workflow may add complexity without enough benefit. If it regularly receives cross-border payments, it may be worth comparing a stablecoin provider's total costs and settlement process with existing alternatives.

A practical checklist before launch

  1. Confirm the provider accepts your business entity and the countries where you operate.
  2. Confirm the exact USDC network and supported wallet or payment instructions.
  3. Get written details of conversion rates, fees, settlement timing and account-credit conditions.
  4. Test invoice matching, payment notifications and accounting exports.
  5. Write a process for wrong-network transfers, duplicate payments, refunds and suspicious transactions.
  6. Ask your accountant and legal or compliance adviser how the activity should be recorded and monitored in your jurisdictions.

Frequently asked questions

Can a business receive USDC and get US dollars in its bank account?

Yes, some providers offer a conversion and bank-deposit arrangement. PNC's limited pilot with Coinbase, announced on 9 November 2026, is one example for eligible corporate and institutional clients.

Does PNC's USDC payment service work for every business?

No. PNC describes it as a limited pilot for eligible Corporate and Institutional Banking clients. Businesses should contact PNC directly to confirm eligibility and availability.

Does USDC always convert to exactly one US dollar?

PNC says its pilot converts incoming USDC 1-to-1 into US dollars. That is a description of this service's announced conversion arrangement, not a guarantee that every USDC provider or exchange will offer the same rate or terms.

Are stablecoin payments cheaper than bank transfers?

Not necessarily. Compare network charges, provider fees, conversion costs, bank fees, foreign-exchange costs and the time until funds are usable. The PNC announcement does not publish a complete fee comparison.

Can a stablecoin payment be reversed like a card payment?

Usually not through the same card-network chargeback process. Businesses should agree on refund and error-handling procedures with their provider before accepting payments.

What this development means

The PNC and Coinbase pilot is a useful example of traditional banking services connecting to stablecoin payment infrastructure. Its practical significance is not simply that a bank accepts a crypto token. It is that an eligible business can receive USDC and have the payment converted into dollars for a designated bank account.

For businesses, the important questions remain operational: who can use the service, what it costs, how quickly funds become available, how payments are reconciled and who handles compliance and exceptions. Those details matter more than the headline announcement.

Finance and fintech

Flat-rate or interchange-plus: how to choose a payment processor

Published by Stackwire. Published 6 November 2026. Updated 10 November 2026.

Your processor touches every sale, so a small difference in fees compounds fast. Here is how to compare options on what you will actually pay.

Quick answer

For a small or low-volume business, flat-rate pricing is usually simpler. As card volume grows, interchange-plus can cost less because you pay the underlying card fees plus a stated processor markup. Compare your own transaction mix, monthly volume and extra fees before switching.

The two main pricing models

Flat-rate bundles everything into one price, commonly around 2.9% plus 30 cents for online cards. It is simple and quick to set up. Interchange-plus passes the card network’s fee through at cost and adds a fixed processor markup, so you can see exactly what you pay for. One 2026 guide puts competitive small-business markups at roughly 0.15% to 0.30% plus a few cents per transaction.

When each one wins

Flat-rate can be easier to forecast, especially for a new or lower-volume business. Interchange-plus may become more attractive as volume grows or when your card mix includes lower-cost transactions, but there is no reliable universal monthly-volume threshold. The break-even point depends on your average ticket, card mix, channel, provider markup and additional fees. Calculate both models using your own recent transaction data.

A worked example (illustrative numbers)

Take $50,000 a month across 1,000 sales. At 2.9% plus $0.30, you pay $1,450 plus $300, or $1,750 (3.5%). On interchange-plus, assume an average interchange of 1.8% ($900), a 0.30% markup ($150) and $0.10 per sale ($100). That totals $1,150 (2.3%), a saving of about $600 a month. Your real interchange will depend on your card mix.

A checklist beyond the headline rate

  • Payout speed: standard payouts often take 1 to 2 business days, and instant payouts usually cost extra.
  • Account holds: ask how the processor handles reserves and fund freezes, a documented risk at higher volumes.
  • Chargeback fees and how disputes are handled.
  • Contract terms: monthly minimums, long contracts and cancellation fees.
  • Fit: marketplaces need split payouts, and SaaS needs solid subscription billing.

What is included in a payment processing fee?

A card payment is not a single fee paid to one company. Depending on the country, payment method and contract, the merchant's total cost can include interchange, card-network assessments, the acquirer's or processor's markup, gateway or platform charges, currency conversion, fraud tools and optional services.

Visa explains that interchange is a transfer fee between the cardholder's bank and the acquiring bank. Merchants generally pay a merchant discount to their financial institution; that merchant discount can include interchange and other processing services. This distinction matters because a merchant does not simply pay Visa's published interchange rate as its entire processing bill.

Flat-rate vs interchange-plus: compare the real bill

Flat-rate pricing combines components into a simpler rate. It is easier to forecast, but the provider's blended rate may be higher than the underlying cost for some card types. Interchange-plus separates the interchange component from the processor's markup. It can improve transparency, but monthly statements may be harder to interpret and the final rate changes with the card mix and transaction qualification.

QuestionFlat-rateInterchange-plus
Can you forecast the fee quickly?Usually easierNeeds transaction mix assumptions
Can you see the processor markup?Usually bundledUsually itemized
Does the cost vary by card type?Often blended into one rateYes, interchange varies
Best comparison inputEffective rate plus extrasInterchange mix plus markup and extras

How to calculate your effective processing rate

Use the same statement period for every provider. Add processing fees and other mandatory payment charges, then divide by the total card volume for that period. Multiply by 100 to get a percentage.

Effective rate formula

(Total processing fees ÷ total processed card volume) × 100 = effective processing rate.

For example, if a business processes $40,000 in card payments and pays $1,160 in total processing fees, its effective rate is 2.9%. This number is more useful than comparing only the headline percentage because it reflects the business's actual transactions and the fees on its statement.

Run a fair provider comparison

  1. Collect at least one representative month of statements, ideally several months if seasonal changes are significant.
  2. Separate card-present, online, keyed, international and recurring transactions.
  3. Record average ticket size, number of transactions, refunds and chargebacks.
  4. Ask each provider to quote the same mix and list every recurring, per-transaction and optional fee.
  5. Model the total cost at current volume and at a realistic growth scenario.
  6. Check contract terms, payout timing, reserve policy and support before making the decision.

Estimate your monthly processing fees

Compare two hypothetical quotes using the same card volume and transaction count. Enter rates from actual provider proposals. This estimate excludes taxes and fees you do not enter; interchange is an assumed average, not a fixed rate.

Flat-rate vs interchange-plus calculator

Illustrative estimate: flat-rate $1,750.00; interchange-plus $1,150.00 including entered monthly fees.

Actual statements may include additional items and different card qualification categories. Use the same statement period and include every applicable fee.

Fees that can change the comparison

  • International cards and currency conversion: these may carry additional fees and should be modelled separately.
  • Manually entered transactions: some providers charge a different rate for keyed payments.
  • Refunds: ask whether the original processing fee is returned when a transaction is refunded.
  • Chargebacks: compare dispute fees, evidence tools and how quickly you must respond.
  • Monthly minimums and platform fees: a low percentage can be offset by fixed monthly charges.
  • Reserves and payout holds: understand when funds can be delayed, what triggers a reserve and how it is released.

Questions to ask before signing

  • Is the quote for domestic consumer cards, or does it include business and international cards?
  • Which fees are pass-through and which are the provider's markup?
  • Are there gateway, PCI, account, minimum-volume or cancellation charges?
  • How are refunds, disputes, failed payments and recurring billing charged?
  • What are the payout schedule, reserve conditions and escalation channels?
  • Can the provider supply a sample statement using my transaction profile?

Frequently asked questions

Is interchange-plus always cheaper?

No. It can be competitive for some businesses, but the outcome depends on card mix, transaction type, processor markup, fixed fees and volume. Compare total cost using your own statements rather than assuming a universal break-even point.

What is an effective rate in payment processing?

It is the total fees paid divided by the total card volume processed over the same period. It gives you a practical blended view of what accepting card payments actually costs.

Do merchants pay interchange directly to Visa?

Not usually as a direct payment to the network. Visa describes interchange as a transfer between issuing and acquiring banks. Merchants pay a merchant discount to their financial institution or acquirer, which can include interchange and other costs.

What payment processor fees should a small business compare?

Compare percentage and per-transaction fees, international and currency conversion charges, refunds, chargebacks, monthly or gateway fees, payout costs and any contract or cancellation charges.

All numbers in the worked example are illustrative, not a provider quote. Fees and eligibility vary by market and contract. Confirm current terms directly before switching.

Payment gateway vs payment processor: what's the difference?

Published by Stackwire. Published 9 November 2026. Updated 10 November 2026.

A payment gateway securely captures and passes payment details. A payment processor handles the transaction communications that help move a payment through banks and card networks. Many modern providers bundle both jobs, which is why the terms are often confused.

Quick answer

A gateway is the secure connection between a checkout and the payment system. A processor carries out the transaction-processing work behind the scenes, including communicating with the relevant financial institutions and networks. A business may buy these services separately or use one payment service provider (PSP) that combines them. The exact division of responsibilities depends on the provider and payment method.

What is a payment gateway?

A payment gateway is the technology that securely collects or receives payment details at checkout and sends the transaction information to the next part of the payment system. For an online store, it connects the website or app to the payment provider. In a physical shop, a point-of-sale terminal and its software perform a related role.

Think of the gateway as the secure entrance and routing layer. It helps transmit the payment request, and may support features such as hosted checkout pages, tokenization, payment-method selection and connections to more than one processor. The features included vary by provider; a gateway is not automatically a complete fraud, compliance or payment-management solution.

What is a payment processor?

A payment processor handles the technical work involved in routing and processing a payment through the payment ecosystem. For a card transaction, this can include communicating with the acquiring side, card network and issuing bank, receiving the authorization response, and supporting clearing and settlement processes.

The processor is part of a wider chain. The customer's bank (the issuer) decides whether to approve or decline the authorization request. The merchant's acquiring bank or acquirer provides the merchant's connection to the card system and receives transaction funds for settlement. The processor helps these parties exchange the information needed to complete the transaction.

Payment gateway vs payment processor: key differences

AreaPayment gatewayPayment processor
Main roleSecurely captures and transmits payment details from checkoutRoutes and processes transaction messages through the payment system
Where it sitsClose to the website, app or point-of-sale checkoutBehind the checkout, connected to acquirers, networks and banks
Typical functionsCheckout connection, data transmission, tokenization or hosted payment fields, depending on providerAuthorization routing, transaction processing and support for clearing and settlement
What it does not automatically meanIt is not necessarily the acquirer or the company holding merchant fundsIt is not necessarily the checkout interface the customer sees
How businesses buy itSeparately or bundled into a broader payment platformSeparately or bundled with gateway, acquiring and other services

Important: these are functional distinctions, not a universal map of every provider's product. Some providers use the word “processor” broadly, while others describe a full-stack platform as a PSP. Always check the actual service agreement and technical documentation rather than relying on the product label alone.

How an online card payment works

Here is a simplified view of a typical online card payment. The exact message flow differs by provider, region, card scheme and checkout setup.

  1. The customer checks out. They enter card details or choose a saved payment method on the merchant's website or app.
  2. The gateway securely handles the payment data. It sends the payment request to the payment platform or processor. Hosted fields and tokenization can help reduce how much raw card data the merchant's systems handle.
  3. The processor routes the authorization request. The request travels through the acquiring side and card network to the cardholder's issuing bank.
  4. The issuer makes an authorization decision. The bank approves or declines based on its checks, available credit or funds, risk signals and other rules.
  5. The response returns to checkout. The response travels back through the payment chain so the merchant can show the customer whether the payment was approved.
  6. Capture, clearing and settlement follow. Depending on the transaction, the merchant captures the authorized payment. The transaction is then cleared and funds are settled through the relevant financial institutions according to their schedules and terms.

An authorization is not the same as money arriving in the merchant's bank account. A payment can be approved first and settled later. Some businesses capture immediately; others authorize first and capture when an order ships or a service is delivered.

Where does a payment service provider (PSP) fit?

A payment service provider, often shortened to PSP, offers a broader package that can combine gateway technology, processing, acquiring connections, payment methods, risk tools, reporting and merchant onboarding. The exact bundle differs between providers.

This is why a business using one integrated platform may not need to contract with a separate gateway and processor. The provider may manage several layers behind one API, dashboard and commercial agreement. That does not mean the gateway and processor have become the same technical function; it means the business is buying a bundled service.

Do you need both a gateway and a processor?

If you accept online card payments, the payment flow needs a way to collect and transmit payment details and a way to process the transaction through the payment system. But you do not necessarily need to select or manage two separate vendors.

  • Small online store: an all-in-one PSP can be simpler to integrate and operate.
  • Established ecommerce business: a separate gateway may make sense if it offers routing flexibility, existing integrations or control over the checkout experience.
  • Marketplace or platform: evaluate connected accounts, split payments, seller onboarding, payout controls and responsibility for disputes.
  • Multi-country business: check local acquiring, supported payment methods, settlement currencies, cross-border fees and regulatory requirements in each market.

Do not choose based on the label alone. Map the services your business actually needs and identify which provider is responsible for each one.

What should you compare before choosing a provider?

The gateway-versus-processor distinction explains the architecture. It does not tell you which provider is the better commercial choice. Compare the full operating cost and the parts of the payment experience that affect your customers.

What to compareQuestions to ask
Total feesWhat are the percentage and fixed transaction fees, monthly charges, gateway fees, cross-border costs, currency conversion charges and dispute fees?
Payment methodsDoes it support the cards, wallets, bank payments and local methods your customers actually use?
Authorization performanceCan it help improve approval rates with network tokens, account updater tools or intelligent routing? Ask how performance is measured.
Security and complianceWhich party handles card-data security responsibilities, tokenization, authentication and PCI DSS requirements? Confirm your own obligations.
IntegrationAre there reliable APIs, plugins, test environments, webhooks and documentation for your platform?
Settlement and cash flowWhen are funds paid out? Are reserves, rolling holds, payout minimums or settlement delays possible under the contract?
Disputes and supportWho provides evidence tools, chargeback notifications and support when a payment fails or is disputed?
Exit and portabilityCan you export customer tokens or payment records where permitted? What happens if you change providers?

Example: choosing between separate services and an all-in-one PSP

Imagine a growing online retailer that already uses a checkout platform but wants to change how card payments are routed. It could keep its current gateway and connect a different processor, if the contracts and integrations support that setup. Alternatively, it could move to a PSP that bundles checkout, processing and acquiring services.

The separate setup may offer more flexibility or preserve an existing checkout, but it can mean more integrations, contracts and support handoffs. The bundled option may simplify operations, but the retailer should check whether it can use the payment methods, routing controls, reporting and commercial terms it needs.

There is no universal winner. Compare the total cost, approval performance, operational workload and ability to change providers. For a related breakdown of pricing models, read how to choose a payment processor.

Compare two payment setups for the same business

Consider an online retailer that sells in its home market and plans to expand internationally. It has two broad options. The right choice depends on the retailer's integration needs, supported markets and operating model, not on whether a provider calls itself a gateway or processor.

Decision areaSeparate gateway and processing partnersIntegrated PSP
Integration workMay require coordinating separate APIs, credentials, contracts and technical support teams.May provide one integration and dashboard for several payment functions.
Routing controlCan offer flexibility if the gateway supports multiple processor connections and the merchant has the required agreements.Routing options depend on the PSP's platform, markets and commercial terms.
International expansionMerchant can select partners for particular markets, but must manage the extra relationships and integrations.One provider may simplify expansion where it supports the target countries, currencies and local payment methods.
Support and accountabilityResponsibility may be split, so the merchant should map who handles checkout, authorization, settlement and disputes.A single provider may reduce handoffs, but the contract still determines responsibility and escalation paths.
Cost comparisonAdd gateway, processing, acquiring, cross-border, currency conversion, dispute and other applicable charges.Review the complete fee schedule and any additional charges; a bundled price is not automatically cheaper.

Before signing, ask each provider to walk through one real transaction from checkout to payout, including a decline, refund and dispute. Request a written fee schedule and confirm which entity is responsible for each operational step. This makes competing proposals easier to compare than headline transaction rates alone.

Common misconceptions

  • “The gateway moves the money.” Usually, the gateway's core role is secure data capture and transmission. The financial institutions and processing/acquiring arrangements handle authorization and settlement.
  • “The processor is the customer's bank.” No. The issuing bank makes the authorization decision for the cardholder's account.
  • “Every business needs two vendors.” No. A PSP can bundle gateway and processing services.
  • “The lowest transaction rate is the cheapest option.” Not necessarily. Monthly charges, fixed fees, international payments, disputes, reserves and conversion costs can change the total.
  • “Approved means settled.” Authorization confirms approval at that stage. Capture, clearing and settlement are separate steps.

Frequently asked questions

Is a payment gateway the same as a payment processor?

No. A gateway securely captures and transmits payment information from checkout. A processor handles transaction processing and communications through the payment ecosystem. Some providers offer both in one platform.

Can I use a payment gateway without a processor?

A gateway alone does not complete a card payment. The transaction still needs processing through an acquirer, processor or integrated payment provider. A gateway vendor may connect you to those services through partners.

Is PayPal a payment gateway or a payment processor?

Product descriptions can cover several roles. PayPal offers a range of payment products, and the functions included depend on the product and market. Check the specific service documentation and agreement to see whether gateway, processing and other services are bundled.

What is the difference between a PSP and a payment gateway?

A gateway is one component that securely transmits payment data. A PSP is a broader provider that may combine gateway, processing, acquiring, payment methods, risk tools and other services.

Does a payment gateway handle refunds and chargebacks?

It depends on the product. A gateway or payment dashboard may provide buttons and APIs for refunds or dispute information, but the actual refund and dispute processes involve the payment provider, acquirer, card network and banks. Confirm who is responsible for each step.

Which is better for a small business?

Many small businesses prefer an integrated PSP because it can reduce setup and vendor management. The right choice depends on supported countries and payment methods, total fees, payout terms, integration needs and support quality.

Bottom line

A payment gateway connects checkout to the payment system and securely transmits payment information. A payment processor handles transaction processing through the relevant financial institutions and networks. A PSP may combine both, along with other services. For a business, the best choice is the setup that provides the payment methods, security, reliability, support and total cost it needs—not simply the product with the most familiar label.

Sources and further reading

  • Adyen: Everything you need to know about payment gateways — gateway and processor roles, merchant accounts and PSPs.
  • Stripe: Payment processor vs payment gateway — an overview of how the services work together.
  • PayPal: What is a payment gateway? — a provider's explanation of gateway and processing services.

This article is for general educational purposes. Payment terminology, responsibilities and regulatory requirements vary by provider, payment method and country. Check your provider's current documentation and contract before making a business decision.

US stablecoin rules: what founders need to know in 2026

Published by Stackwire. Published 6 November 2026. Updated 10 November 2026.

The first US federal stablecoin law is moving from paper to practice. If you build, accept or hold stablecoins, here is where things stand and what to check now.

Quick answer

The US GENIUS Act created a federal framework for payment stablecoin issuers. Founders should check an issuer's regulatory status, reserve disclosures, redemption terms and compliance obligations before relying on a stablecoin. This is general information, not legal advice.

IN THIS GUIDE

  1. Where the rules stand
  2. Implementation timeline: what is final and what is still pending?
  3. What issuers must do
  4. Why it matters even if you never issue a coin
  5. A five-point check for founders
  6. What the OCC's October 2026 final rule covers
  7. Are stablecoin issuer applications open yet?
  8. What founders should distinguish
  9. A practical due-diligence checklist
  10. What the law does not tell a founder automatically
  11. Frequently asked questions
  12. Sources

Where the rules stand

The GENIUS Act became law in July 2025. It created a federal licensing framework for payment stablecoin issuers, with reserve, audit and anti-money-laundering requirements. The OCC issued its final rule on October 21, 2026 for payment stablecoin issuers and related activities within its jurisdiction. That rule is scheduled to take effect on January 18, 2027. It covers reserve assets, redemption, risk management, audits, reporting, supervision and custody. It does not complete every part of the federal implementation: the OCC says Bank Secrecy Act, anti-money-laundering and sanctions requirements are being handled in separate rulemaking with Treasury. The GENIUS Act was enacted on July 18, 2025, and the OCC describes January 18, 2027 as the effective date for the Act and its final rule.

Implementation timeline: what is final and what is still pending?

DateDevelopmentWhat it means
18 July 2025GENIUS Act enactedFederal statutory framework for payment stablecoins was established.
21 October 2026OCC issued its final ruleFinal OCC rules address issuers and activities within OCC jurisdiction, plus certain custody activities.
18 January 2027Act and OCC final rule effectiveKey statutory and OCC implementation requirements take effect on this date.
As of 10 November 2026OCC applications not yet openThe OCC says it will announce when it can accept applications and waiver requests after required information-collection approval.

The OCC rule is not a single nationwide answer for every stablecoin company. The regulator depends on the issuer's legal status and the activity involved. The OCC also says separate rulemaking will address Bank Secrecy Act, anti-money-laundering and sanctions provisions within its implementation work.

What issuers must do

  • Maintain eligible reserve assets that meet the GENIUS Act and applicable regulator rules. Do not assume a token is compliant simply because its issuer publishes a reserve statement.
  • Honor redemptions at par.
  • Meet applicable audit, reporting and supervisory requirements. AML and sanctions implementation details are being handled through separate rulemaking and other applicable obligations.
  • An issuer may not pay interest or yield solely for holding a payment stablecoin. This is not the same as saying every third-party rewards arrangement is automatically permitted; the legal and economic structure matters and requires specialist review.

Why it matters even if you never issue a coin

Using a stablecoin in the US will increasingly depend on the regulatory status of the company behind it. Exchanges, wallets and payment firms that support a token take on risk if its issuer is unlicensed or cannot show its reserves.

A five-point check for founders

  1. Confirm the issuer’s license status or the pathway it is using.
  2. Read the latest reserve attestation and the redemption terms.
  3. Check how the token fits your AML and KYC flows.
  4. Get legal review before advertising any yield or rewards on stablecoin balances.
  5. Plan for other markets: the UK expects FCA authorization for issuers whose tokens circulate there, and the EU already enforces MiCA licensing.

What the OCC's October 2026 final rule covers

The OCC's October 21 bulletin says its final rule implements the GENIUS Act for entities under OCC jurisdiction. The rule covers permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers within that scope, as well as certain custody activities by OCC-supervised entities. It sets standards for reserve assets, redemption, risk management, audits, reports, supervision, applications and registrations.

Do not read an OCC rule as a complete answer for every stablecoin business. Different issuers may fall under different primary federal or state regulators, and separate Treasury and agency work remains relevant. A wallet, exchange, payment company or software provider may have a different regulatory role from the issuer itself.

Are stablecoin issuer applications open yet?

As of November 10, 2026, the OCC's GENIUS Act landing page says it is not yet accepting applications or waiver requests. It says applications will begin after the Office of Management and Budget gives final approval to the information collection for application forms, and the OCC will announce when the process opens. This is a time-sensitive status and should be rechecked before relying on it.

What founders should distinguish

  • Issuer: the entity that creates and redeems the payment stablecoin and is subject to issuer requirements.
  • Custodian: the entity that safeguards reserve assets or customer stablecoins, depending on the service and legal arrangement.
  • Exchange or wallet: a service that may distribute, hold or facilitate transfers of a token without being its issuer.
  • Merchant or SaaS business: a company that accepts stablecoins as payment and must assess payment, custody, sanctions and jurisdictional questions relevant to its own activities.

These labels are not legal conclusions. A company's actual activities, control over customer assets, location and contractual structure determine which rules may apply.

A practical due-diligence checklist

  1. Identify the legal entity that issues the token. Do not rely only on the brand name or ticker.
  2. Check whether the issuer is permitted under the relevant US framework, or whether an applicable transition or waiver process is in place.
  3. Read reserve disclosures and independent attestations. Check what assets back the token, where they are held and how frequently information is published.
  4. Read redemption terms, including who can redeem, minimum amounts, fees, timing and circumstances where redemption can be delayed.
  5. Map the service providers in the flow: issuer, custodian, exchange, wallet, payment processor and banking partners.
  6. Document sanctions screening, transaction monitoring, suspicious activity escalation and recordkeeping responsibilities with qualified counsel.
  7. Check the rules in every country where customers, counterparties or operations are located. A US framework does not replace local licensing requirements elsewhere.

What the law does not tell a founder automatically

The existence of a federal framework does not mean every token described as a stablecoin is approved, every issuer is licensed, or every platform offering a token has the same regulatory status. It also does not remove operational risks such as smart-contract vulnerabilities, depegging, custody failures, banking interruptions or redemption bottlenecks.

For product teams, the right question is not simply “Is this a stablecoin?” It is “Who issues it, what rights does the holder have, how can it be redeemed, who controls the keys and reserves, and which rules apply to each party in our flow?”

Frequently asked questions

What is the GENIUS Act?

The GENIUS Act is a US federal law enacted on July 18, 2025 that creates a framework for payment stablecoin issuers. It establishes requirements around permitted issuers, reserves, redemption and supervision, with implementation by federal and state regulators.

When does the OCC's GENIUS Act final rule take effect?

The OCC's October 21, 2026 final rule states an effective date of January 18, 2027. The scope is limited to issuers and activities under OCC jurisdiction; other agencies have separate implementation responsibilities.

Can a company issue a payment stablecoin in the United States today?

The GENIUS Act generally requires a person issuing a payment stablecoin in the United States to be a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, subject to the Act's terms and transition provisions. Businesses should obtain current legal advice rather than infer permission from a token's market availability.

Does the GENIUS Act make stablecoins risk-free?

No. Regulation can set issuer and reserve standards, but it does not remove market, operational, cyber, custody, liquidity or counterparty risks. Review the token's issuer, reserve information and redemption rights.

This is general educational information, not legal or financial advice. Rules and application status can change; consult qualified counsel and the relevant regulator before acting.

  • OCC News Release 2026-92 — October 21, 2026 final-rule announcement and effective date.
  • OCC GENIUS Act implementation page — current application and waiver status.

SaaS and AI

How can businesses let AI agents make payments safely?

Published by Stackwire. Published 10 November 2026.

AI agents are starting to handle business payment tasks, not just research and repetitive admin. But before a company lets an agent pay an invoice, it needs to decide exactly what the agent is allowed to do.

Quick answer

Businesses should give AI agents limited permissions, not unrestricted access to company money. Set payment limits, verify suppliers, separate payment preparation from approval, protect credentials and record every transaction.

AI agents are moving into business payments

Imagine a company that receives 200 supplier invoices every month. An employee usually checks each invoice, confirms the supplier, opens a payment portal and enters the payment details.

An AI agent could help with several of these steps. It could find an invoice, compare it with purchase records, prepare a payment and submit it after the required approval.

This is moving beyond theory. On October 20, 2026, Visa, BILL and Billtrust announced a live pilot in which trusted AI agents can initiate and complete buyer-approved invoice payments through supplier portals.

The pilot uses Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol, tokenized payment credentials and controls connected to the buyer's approved payment instructions. Visa says the agent executes eligible payments that have already been approved by the buyer; it does not make the payment decision itself.

Read Visa's announcement.

How should an AI agent payment work?

A business should decide what an agent can do before connecting it to a payment system. For example, it may allow an agent to read invoices from approved suppliers, match them against purchase orders, prepare payment requests and record completed transactions.

That does not mean the agent should also be able to change supplier bank details, increase its own spending limit or approve unusual payments.

What if a supplier changes its bank details?

Imagine a company normally pays a supplier $2,000 each month. The next invoice has the same supplier name, but a different bank account number.

The agent should not treat the familiar name as proof that the new details are genuine. It should pause the payment and request verification through a trusted contact method already on file, rather than relying on the email or invoice that requested the change.

The same rule should apply to duplicate invoices, unexpected amounts and requests to pay a new recipient. An instruction inside an email or invoice is information to check, not automatic permission to move money.

Five controls every business should consider

1. Set clear payment limits

Define maximum amounts per transaction and over a set period. A company might allow an agent to prepare any payment but only execute transactions that meet a pre-approved policy.

2. Verify suppliers and payment details

Maintain approved supplier records. A change to a bank account, payment destination or supplier identity should trigger an independent verification process.

3. Separate preparation from approval

An agent that prepares a payment should not automatically have permission to approve it. Keep approval authority separate, especially for large or unusual transactions.

4. Protect payment credentials

Avoid giving agents unrestricted access to bank accounts, card details or employee login credentials. Use appropriately restricted credentials and payment infrastructure. In Visa's announced pilot, tokenized payment credentials are used instead of sharing supplier-portal logins.

5. Keep an audit trail

Record the invoice, payment request, authorization, agent identity, approval and final transaction result. Finance teams should be able to understand what happened without relying only on the agent's explanation.

What are Google's AP2 and Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol?

Companies are developing different approaches to make agent-led payments more trustworthy.

Google's Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) is an open protocol designed to represent payment instructions and authorization. On April 28, 2026, Google announced that it was donating AP2 to the FIDO Alliance and releasing AP2 v0.2, which adds support for autonomous transactions based on instructions authorized in advance, including payments when the user is not present.

Read Google's AP2 announcement.

Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol focuses on helping merchants recognize and authenticate legitimate AI agents. Its developer documentation describes how merchants can validate signed agent requests.

Read Visa's developer documentation.

These initiatives address related but different parts of the problem. AP2 represents authorized payment intent, while Visa's protocol focuses on agent recognition and authentication. Neither replaces a company's own fraud checks, approval procedures or financial controls.

What should businesses do before adopting AI payments?

Businesses do not need to start by allowing an agent to control every payment. A safer starting point is one limited workflow with a small group of verified suppliers.

  • Choose one low-risk payment process.
  • Define exactly what the agent can access and execute.
  • Keep human approval for exceptions and unusual transactions.
  • Test duplicate invoices and changed bank details.
  • Monitor failed and suspicious payment attempts.
  • Review permissions regularly and maintain a way to stop the agent.

The PCI Security Standards Council published additional guidance on securing AI in payment environments on October 7, 2026. The guidance discusses securing AI deployments while maintaining appropriate payment security controls.

Read the PCI SSC announcement.

Final thoughts

AI agents could make business payments faster by reducing manual work in accounts payable. But faster payments are not automatically safer payments.

A reliable system needs clear authorization, verified suppliers, restricted credentials and a way to stop unusual transactions.

The goal is not to give an AI agent control over company money. It is to let the agent complete specific, approved tasks while the business keeps control.

Frequently asked questions

Can AI agents make payments without human approval?

Some systems can execute payments under instructions authorized in advance. Whether a payment can proceed without a person depends on the payment system and the business's approval rules.

What is an AI agent payment?

It is a payment initiated or completed by an AI agent acting on behalf of a person or business, within the permissions it has been given.

How can businesses prevent AI payment fraud?

They can verify suppliers, restrict payment permissions, set transaction limits, independently check changed bank details and monitor payment activity.

What is Google's AP2 protocol?

AP2 is an open protocol designed to help represent authorization and trust for payments initiated by AI agents.

Does Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol approve payments?

Its role is to help merchants recognize and authenticate trusted agents. Payment authorization and business spending rules remain separate considerations.

Should small businesses use AI agents for payments?

They can explore limited, low-risk automation, but should first establish supplier verification, approval procedures, secure payment access and transaction monitoring.

Sources and further reading

  • Google: AP2 donation to the FIDO Alliance — April 28, 2026.
  • Visa: Trusted Agent Protocol documentation.
  • PCI Security Standards Council: AI in payment environments — October 7, 2026.

This article explains general technology and operational practices. It is not legal, financial or payment-security compliance advice. Check the requirements that apply to your business and jurisdiction.

SaaS and AI

How to calculate AI API costs before you ship a feature

Published by Stackwire. Published 9 November 2026. Updated 10 November 2026.

An AI feature can look inexpensive in a demo and become a margin problem after customers use it every day. The fix is not guesswork. Estimate the cost of one completed task, multiply it by realistic usage, then test the assumptions against real API logs.

Quick answer

To estimate AI API cost, multiply input tokens and output tokens by their respective per-token prices, add any tool, image, audio or other charges, and include retries and failed requests. Calculate the result per successful customer task, then multiply by expected monthly tasks. Always use the provider's current pricing page for the model and features you actually deploy.

1. Start with the unit: one completed task

Do not begin with a monthly budget. Begin with a single task your customer understands: one support reply drafted, one document summarized, one product description generated or one report created.

Define what counts as complete. If the workflow makes three model calls, searches a knowledge base and retries when the output is invalid, the cost of the task is not the cost of one model call. It is the cost of the whole workflow that produced the accepted result.

Write down the steps in order. For each step, record the model, input tokens, output tokens, any cached input, and any non-token charges. Keep successful and failed attempts separate so you can see where waste occurs.

2. Understand what the API bills for

For text models, providers commonly publish separate prices for input and output tokens. Input includes the instructions, conversation history, retrieved text and user message sent to the model. Output is the text the model generates. Output tokens can cost more per million than input tokens, so a long answer may cost more than expected.

One token is not the same as one word or one character. Token counts depend on the language, formatting and content. Measure tokens using the provider's tokenizer or actual usage fields from API responses rather than estimating from word count.

Some workflows have additional billable components. Depending on the provider and model, these can include image or audio processing, web search, tool calls, batch processing, long-context tiers or other hosted services. Read the model-specific pricing notes, not just the headline input price.

3. Use this simple cost formula

Text-model estimate

Request cost = (input tokens ÷ 1,000,000 × input price per million) + (output tokens ÷ 1,000,000 × output price per million) + other billable charges.

Then calculate the workflow cost:

  • Expected cost per completed task = average cost of all attempts needed to produce one accepted result.
  • Monthly API cost = expected cost per completed task × completed tasks per month.
  • Monthly cost per active customer = monthly API cost ÷ active customers in the same period.

For a workflow with multiple model calls, calculate each call separately and add them together. Do not apply one average token count to every step if the steps behave differently.

4. Try the AI API cost calculator

Enter your estimated token usage and the prices shown on your provider's current pricing page. The calculator uses prices per one million tokens and estimates text-model charges only. It does not include tools, media, taxes, hosting or retries unless you increase the token totals to account for them.

Estimate your API spend

Estimated monthly text-model cost: $31.00
Estimated cost per request: $0.0031

Illustrative starting values only. Replace them with current provider rates and measured token usage. This estimate assumes one model request per task and excludes all other charges.

5. A worked example (illustrative, not a provider quote)

Imagine a SaaS product generates a short customer-support draft. For one model request, assume it uses 1,500 input tokens and 400 output tokens. To make the arithmetic easy, assume a hypothetical model price of $1 per million input tokens and $4 per million output tokens.

ComponentCalculationCost
Input1,500 ÷ 1,000,000 × $1$0.0015
Output400 ÷ 1,000,000 × $4$0.0016
Total for one request$0.0015 + $0.0016$0.0031
10,000 requests10,000 × $0.0031$31.00

This is only a worked calculation. The assumed rates are not current market prices, and the example excludes retries, tools, taxes and infrastructure. Replace the assumptions with the exact prices and measured usage for your chosen model before making a business decision.

Now add workflow reality. If some drafts need a second attempt, or the system makes a separate classification call first, the real cost per accepted draft will be higher. Measure the average number of attempts and calls per completed task from production logs.

6. Five cost drivers teams often miss

Long prompts and conversation history

Sending the full conversation, policy instructions or document on every request can make input usage grow quietly. Keep only the context needed for the task, summarize older conversation when appropriate, and avoid repeating static instructions unnecessarily.

Output length

Asking for a detailed explanation, multiple alternatives or verbose structured output increases generated tokens. Set a useful output limit and ask for the format the product actually needs. Do not make answers shorter at the expense of task quality; measure both cost and acceptance rate.

Retries and validation loops

Retries can multiply cost, especially when the same large prompt is sent again. Track why requests fail: timeouts, invalid JSON, safety refusals, poor retrieval or unclear instructions. Fix the cause rather than automatically increasing retries.

Prompt caching

When supported, prompt caching can reduce the price of repeated prompt prefixes. It is most useful when requests share a stable prefix, such as long system instructions or reference material. Cache writes and reads may have different prices and time windows, so check the provider's documentation and measure cache-hit rates. Caching does not make new user input or generated output free.

Tools and non-text inputs

Search, code execution, image understanding, audio and other tools can have separate charges. Add them to the workflow estimate rather than treating every AI feature as a single text-model call.

7. Turn the estimate into a monthly budget

Build three usage scenarios instead of relying on one optimistic forecast:

  • Low: expected adoption with light usage per customer.
  • Base: the usage level you would plan operations around.
  • High: a realistic heavy-use case, not an impossible worst case.

For each scenario, estimate active customers, completed tasks per customer, average calls per task and cost per call. Add a separate allowance for non-token charges. The high-use scenario is especially important if your plan includes unlimited or generous AI usage.

After launch, replace assumptions with observed data. Review average and 95th-percentile cost per task, cost per active customer, retry rate, cache-hit rate and the share of tasks that require human correction. An average can hide a small group of very expensive customers.

8. Choose the right optimization, not just the cheapest model

Try optimizations in this order:

  1. Remove unnecessary context and repeated instructions.
  2. Set output limits that match the product experience.
  3. Reduce avoidable retries by improving prompts, retrieval and validation.
  4. Use caching or batch processing when the workload and provider support it.
  5. Test a less expensive model on representative tasks and compare quality, latency and completion rate.

A cheaper model is not automatically cheaper for the business if it produces more incorrect answers, retries or support tickets. Compare cost per accepted result, not only cost per API call.

9. Connect cost to your pricing model

Once you know cost per completed task, you can decide what to include in each subscription tier. A base allowance with metered overages can make costs more predictable for both sides. A credit system can work when tasks have different costs, but explain what a credit represents. Avoid unlimited usage unless you have evidence that heavy users remain profitable.

For the next step, read our guide to pricing an AI feature without losing your margins. It covers hybrid plans and how to think about allowances and overages.

Frequently asked questions

How do I calculate the cost of one AI API request?

Multiply input tokens by the input rate and output tokens by the output rate, using the provider's published units. Add any billable tools, media or other features. Check actual usage data from the API response.

How much does 1,000 AI requests cost?

There is no universal price. It depends on the model, token counts, input and output rates, caching and tools. Estimate one representative request first, then multiply by 1,000. Use real usage rather than request count alone.

Does prompt caching make AI API calls free?

No. Caching can reduce the cost of eligible repeated input, but cache writes, new input, generated output and other billable components may still be charged. Check the provider's current cache pricing and usage reports.

Should SaaS companies charge per AI request?

Not always. A fixed allowance, usage-based overage or credit system can work depending on how predictable the task costs are and how customers understand the value. Test the model against actual usage distribution and support expectations.

  • OpenAI prompt caching guide — how cache reuse works and how it affects cost.
  • Anthropic Claude pricing — input/output, caching and other pricing details.

Provider prices and product terms can change. Check the official pricing documentation on the date you estimate costs. This article is educational and is not financial or legal advice.
