SaaS and AI

How much does an AI agent cost? A practical cost breakdown

Published by Stackwire. Published 9 November 2026. Updated 10 November 2026.

An AI agent can make one model call or run a multi-step workflow involving search, tools, memory and retries. That is why the price of the model alone is a poor estimate of what an agent costs. To budget accurately, calculate the cost of a completed task from the full workflow.

Quick answer

AI agent cost depends on model input and output tokens, the number of model calls, paid tools, retrieval or search, storage and compute, retries, and human review. Map one typical task, measure every step, calculate the average cost per successful completion, then multiply by expected monthly tasks.

Why an AI agent costs more than one prompt

A simple chatbot may send a message to a model and return the answer. An agent can decide what to do next, call a tool, inspect the result, ask the model to reason again and repeat until the task is complete. Each model invocation can create token charges, and tools may have their own pricing.

For example, a research agent might classify a request, search a knowledge base, open two sources, summarize them and produce a final response. Counting only the final response misses the earlier model calls and external services.

List every cost component

ComponentWhat to measure
Model callsInput tokens, output tokens, model choice and number of calls
Tool usageSearch, code execution, browser, external APIs and per-call charges
RetrievalEmbedding generation, vector database reads/writes and retrieved context
Memory and storageDatabase, logs, file storage and retention
InfrastructureCompute, orchestration, queues, networking and monitoring
Retries and failuresRepeated calls, timeouts, invalid outputs and abandoned tasks
Human reviewMinutes spent checking or correcting agent output

Some items are fixed monthly costs, while others scale with each task. Keep them separate in your spreadsheet so you do not accidentally count a monthly platform subscription as a per-request fee.

Calculate the model cost for each step

For each model invocation, use the provider's current input and output prices:

Model call cost

(Input tokens ÷ 1,000,000 × input price per million) + (Output tokens ÷ 1,000,000 × output price per million).

Repeat this calculation for every call in the workflow. If a model call uses cached input, a batch rate or a special context tier, apply the relevant price category rather than treating all tokens as identical. The provider's usage response is more reliable than estimating token counts from word counts.

For a deeper explanation, read our guide to calculating AI API costs before shipping a feature.

A worked example: one agent task

Suppose an internal research agent completes a task using three model calls. The following prices and usage are hypothetical and are included only to demonstrate the arithmetic. They are not current provider rates.

StepInput tokensOutput tokensAssumed cost
Plan the task2,000300$0.0032
Review retrieved evidence5,000500$0.0070
Write final result3,000800$0.0062
Total model charges10,0001,600$0.0164

Now add hypothetical tool and infrastructure costs of $0.02 per task. The estimated total is $0.0364 per completed task before human review and shared monthly platform costs. At 10,000 completed tasks, the variable total would be $364. Replace every assumption with measured usage and the exact rates for your selected providers.

Do not forget unsuccessful runs

Agents do not always finish on the first attempt. A tool may fail, the model may return an invalid argument, the search may return poor evidence or a task may exceed its time limit. If you measure only successful low-cost traces, you will understate the budget.

Track cost for every run, including failures. Then calculate:

  • Cost per attempt: total variable cost divided by all attempts.
  • Cost per successful task: total variable cost divided by completed tasks that meet your quality criteria.
  • Success rate: successful tasks divided by all attempts.
  • Human correction rate: completed tasks that need material human changes divided by completed tasks.

The cost per successful task is often the most useful business metric. A cheap agent that fails frequently may cost more than a higher-priced model that completes the task reliably.

Estimate cost per successful agent task

Enter total model and tool cost for one attempt, your observed success rate, and expected monthly completed tasks. The estimate accounts for paid failed attempts by dividing average attempt cost by the success rate.

AI agent task-cost calculator

Estimated variable spend: $404.44 per month
Estimated cost per successful task: $0.0404

Assumes attempts have similar average cost and each unsuccessful attempt is paid for. Real workflows may have different costs for failed and successful runs, so use production trace data when available.

Build three monthly scenarios

Estimate monthly usage at three levels. Keep the assumptions visible rather than hiding them in one total.

ScenarioTasks/monthCost/taskVariable cost
Low1,000$0.0364$36.40
Base10,000$0.0364$364.00
High50,000$0.0364$1,820.00

This simple scenario holds unit cost constant. Real agent costs may rise with longer conversations, more tool calls, bigger documents or heavier customers. Build a separate high-usage unit-cost assumption if your product's usage distribution supports it.

Ways to reduce agent costs without damaging quality

  1. Remove unnecessary steps. Ask whether every planning or reflection call changes the final result. Do not add model calls just because an agent framework makes them easy.
  2. Use the right model for each task. A small classification step may not need the same model as a complex final synthesis. Test quality before switching.
  3. Limit tool loops. Set clear stop conditions, timeouts and maximum tool calls. Give the agent a useful fallback when a tool fails.
  4. Retrieve less, but better. Return relevant passages rather than entire documents. Evaluate retrieval quality so context reduction does not remove necessary evidence.
  5. Cache repeatable work. Cache stable outputs or repeated context where it is safe and supported. Respect freshness and user permissions.
  6. Measure before optimizing. Compare cost per successful task and quality, not just raw token spend.

How to monitor agent cost in production

Log a task ID, customer or tenant identifier, model name, token usage, tool name, tool duration, retries, final status and human review outcome. Avoid logging sensitive customer content unless you have a clear lawful purpose, retention policy and access controls.

Build a dashboard for cost per task, cost per customer, success rate, tool error rate, average steps, p95 latency and human correction rate. Set alerts for sudden changes, such as a spike in model calls per task or a loop that repeatedly invokes the same tool.

Evaluate agent quality with a representative set of real tasks. A change that reduces cost but lowers accuracy or increases human review may not be an improvement. See the OpenAI evaluation best practices for guidance on creating task-specific tests.

Frequently asked questions

How much does one AI agent task cost?

There is no universal price. A short single-call task can be inexpensive, while a multi-step agent with search, tools, large context and retries can cost considerably more. Measure the full workflow and divide by successful completions.

Are AI agents more expensive than chatbots?

They can be, because agents may make multiple model calls and use external tools. But a well-designed agent can also complete a valuable workflow that would otherwise require substantial manual work. Compare total cost with the value and quality of the completed task.

What is the biggest cost driver for an AI agent?

It depends on the workflow. Model calls and long context can dominate, but paid search, external APIs, compute, retries or human review may be material. Instrument the system before assuming which component is largest.

How do I set a budget for an AI agent?

Measure representative tasks, estimate cost per successful completion, model low/base/high monthly volume, include fixed platform costs and set alerts for abnormal usage. Recalculate after significant prompt, model or workflow changes.

Can I use a cheaper model to reduce agent costs?

Possibly. Test the cheaper model on representative tasks and compare success, factual accuracy, tool selection, latency and human correction. The lowest API price is not necessarily the lowest cost per successful task.

  • OpenAI API pricing — current model and tool prices.
  • Anthropic API pricing — model, caching and batch pricing.
  • OpenAI agent evaluations — evaluate agent workflow traces.
  • OpenAI evaluation best practices — design task-specific quality checks.

All figures in the worked examples are illustrative, not provider quotes. Check official pricing for the exact model, region, tools and billing terms you use.

SaaS and AI

RAG vs fine-tuning: which should you use for an AI application?

Published by Stackwire. Published 9 November 2026. Updated 10 November 2026.

If an AI assistant gives outdated answers or ignores your preferred format, you may be looking at two very different problems. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) gives a model access to external information at answer time. Fine-tuning changes model behavior through additional training. Choosing the right approach can save engineering time and avoid unnecessary infrastructure.

Quick answer

Start with RAG when an application must answer questions from private, current or frequently updated documents and show where information came from. Consider fine-tuning when the model consistently needs a specific style, format or task behavior. Combine them only when evaluation shows you need both current knowledge and specialized behavior.

What is RAG?

RAG stands for retrieval-augmented generation. Before the model writes an answer, the application searches a knowledge source, selects relevant passages and includes them in the model's context. The model then generates a response using that retrieved material.

A basic RAG flow looks like this:

  1. A user asks a question.
  2. The application searches an index or knowledge base for relevant passages.
  3. The retriever returns selected text and metadata, such as document title or URL.
  4. The application adds those passages to the model prompt.
  5. The model produces an answer, ideally with references to the supporting sources.

The model's weights are not updated when a document is added. The knowledge base and index are maintained separately. This makes RAG useful when company policies, product documentation or other source material changes over time.

What is fine-tuning?

Fine-tuning is additional training on examples that demonstrate the behavior you want from a model. Depending on the model and training method, it can help with a repeated task, response style, specialized format or domain-specific pattern.

Fine-tuning is not the same as uploading a folder of documents for the model to search. Training examples can influence the model's behavior, but a fine-tuned model does not automatically provide a reliable, traceable copy of every fact in those documents. If a policy changes, you need to consider whether the training data and model need to be updated.

RAG vs fine-tuning: the practical comparison

QuestionRAGFine-tuning
What changes?Information supplied at request timeModel weights through additional training
Best fitAnswering from private or changing knowledgeConsistent task behavior, style or format
Fresh informationUpdate the source and indexMay require new training and deployment
Source citationsCan return retrieved source referencesNot provided automatically
InfrastructureIngestion, indexing and retrievalTraining data, training workflow and model management
Common failureRetrieves irrelevant or incomplete contextLearns inconsistent patterns or fails to generalize

When should you choose RAG?

RAG is a strong starting point when the answer depends on information that is private, long, detailed or regularly updated. Examples include:

  • A customer support assistant that answers from current product manuals.
  • An internal company assistant that searches approved policies and procedures.
  • A SaaS product that answers questions using each customer's uploaded documents.
  • A research assistant that needs to show the sources behind an answer.
  • A help centre chatbot whose content team updates articles every week.

RAG also gives you a place to enforce document-level permissions. The application should filter retrieval based on the signed-in user's access rights. Do not assume that adding a vector database automatically makes private information secure.

When should you consider fine-tuning?

Fine-tuning becomes more relevant when the application has a repeatable task and you have good examples of desired outputs. Consider testing it when:

  • The model repeatedly misses a strict output format despite clear instructions.
  • You need consistent classification or extraction behavior for a narrow task.
  • Your product has a well-defined writing style or response pattern.
  • You have enough representative, reviewed examples to train and evaluate the change.

Do not fine-tune just because an answer is wrong. First check whether the model received the right facts, whether the prompt was clear and whether the task is suitable for the model. Fine-tuning cannot reliably compensate for missing or outdated source information.

Why RAG can still give incorrect answers

RAG is not a guarantee of factual accuracy. The retrieval system may return the wrong passage, miss the relevant document, retrieve stale content or include so much text that the useful detail gets lost. The model can also misunderstand the retrieved material.

Measure retrieval and answer quality separately. Ask whether the correct source was found, whether the selected passage supports the answer, whether the answer uses only supported claims and whether the citation points to the right place. Build a test set from real questions and known correct sources.

Can you use RAG and fine-tuning together?

Yes. A hybrid system can retrieve up-to-date facts with RAG and use a fine-tuned model to perform a specialized task or follow a consistent output pattern. But it adds complexity: you must maintain retrieval, training data, model versions and evaluation for the combined system.

Use a hybrid architecture only when you can identify two separate needs. For example, a support assistant may need to retrieve the latest policy and consistently format its answer into a required support template. RAG addresses the current policy; fine-tuning may help with the repeated response behavior.

A practical decision matrix

Use the problem you need to solve, not the popularity of a technique, to choose an architecture. This matrix is a starting point; validate the choice with representative tests.

Your requirementBest first testWhy
Answers must reflect documents updated every weekRAGUpdate the approved source and refresh its index instead of retraining for each content change.
Answers must quote or link to approved source materialRAGRetrieved passages can carry document IDs, titles and URLs that the application can display as evidence.
Every response must follow a narrow output schemaPrompting and structured outputs first; then evaluate fine-tuningFirst establish whether the model and interface can enforce the format without training.
Classifying a repeated type of request consistentlyEvaluate prompting, then fine-tuningA reviewed set of representative input/output examples can show whether training improves consistency.
Current facts plus a specialized response formatRAG first, then test a hybridRetrieval supplies current evidence; a behavior technique may help format the response if tests show a remaining gap.
The model lacks reliable facts because the source material is missingFix the knowledge source firstNeither retrieval nor training can create trustworthy source evidence that the team does not have.

Worked scenario: a SaaS support assistant

Imagine a software company has a help centre, release notes and account-specific support policies. Customers ask questions such as, “Does my plan include audit-log exports?” The answer can change when the company updates its plans.

RAG approach: index the approved help articles and plan documentation, retrieve passages relevant to the customer's plan, and pass those passages to the model. Store the source title and URL with each passage so the interface can show where the answer came from. Apply account permissions before retrieval, not after the model has already seen the data.

Fine-tuning approach: if the assistant has the correct policy but repeatedly ignores a required support format, collect reviewed examples of the desired format and test whether fine-tuning improves the result. Do not use training as a substitute for retrieving the latest plan terms.

Evaluation: prepare test questions for current plans, retired plans, missing documentation and users without permission. Score whether the correct document was retrieved, the answer matches it, the citation is correct and the assistant declines when evidence is missing. Compare quality, latency and total cost before choosing the production design.

A decision checklist before you build

  1. Write down what is actually wrong: missing facts, poor retrieval, inconsistent format or weak task performance.
  2. Collect 30–100 representative questions and the expected evidence or outputs. This is a starting dataset, not a universal statistical threshold.
  3. Try a clear prompt and a small RAG prototype if private or current information is needed.
  4. Measure retrieval relevance, factual support, citation correctness, latency and cost.
  5. Consider fine-tuning only if the remaining failure is a repeatable behavior problem and you have suitable examples.
  6. Re-run the same tests after every significant prompt, model, retrieval or training change.

Frequently asked questions

Is RAG better than fine-tuning?

Neither is universally better. RAG is usually the more direct starting point for question-answering over changing or private documents. Fine-tuning is aimed at improving specific model behaviors. Choose based on the failure you need to fix.

Does RAG train the AI model?

No. RAG retrieves external information and adds it to the model's input at request time. The underlying model weights are not changed by ordinary retrieval.

Does fine-tuning add company knowledge to a model?

Training can influence how a model responds to examples, but it is not a dependable document lookup system and does not automatically provide citations. For frequently updated company facts, use a controlled knowledge source and retrieval.

Is RAG cheaper than fine-tuning?

It depends on usage, model choice, retrieval infrastructure, training costs and maintenance. RAG adds retrieval and context tokens to requests. Fine-tuning may involve dataset preparation, training and model hosting costs. Compare total cost for your actual workload.

Can a RAG chatbot hallucinate?

Yes. It can retrieve irrelevant passages or generate claims that the retrieved material does not support. Test retrieval quality, require evidence-based answers and provide a safe way to say when the source material is insufficient.

Primary documentation and further reading

  • AWS Prescriptive Guidance: Comparing RAG and fine-tuning
  • Microsoft Learn: RAG and indexes
  • OpenAI: Optimizing LLM accuracy
  • OpenAI: Evaluation best practices

This guide is educational. Architecture, security and compliance decisions depend on the application and data involved.

SaaS and AI

How to price an AI feature without losing your margins

Published by Stackwire. Published 6 November 2026. Updated 10 November 2026.

Classic SaaS had predictable costs. AI does not: every request you serve has a model bill behind it. Here is how to price an AI feature so heavy users do not eat your margin.

Quick answer

A practical way to price an AI feature is a hybrid plan: charge a base subscription, include a defined amount of AI usage, then charge for usage above that allowance. Measure your real cost per task first, and make usage visible so customers are not surprised.

Why seats alone fall short

Traditional SaaS margins were stable because infrastructure cost barely changed per user. With AI, cost follows usage. Two customers on the same seat price can cost you very different amounts, and the heaviest user is often the one who loves the feature most.

A practical starting point: compare hybrid pricing

A hybrid plan is one option worth testing: a base subscription with a defined AI allowance, followed by metered usage or credits when customers go beyond it. It can balance predictable revenue with usage-linked costs, but it is not right for every product. Pure usage pricing may fit developer tools or workloads with clearly measurable consumption. Seat-based pricing can still work when usage is light, consistent or bundled into a broader product benefit. Choose after comparing customer expectations, actual cost distribution and willingness to pay.

A worked example (illustrative numbers)

Say one AI task costs you $0.04 in model fees. A customer running 500 tasks a month costs you $20, and one running 5,000 costs you $200. If both pay the same $30 seat, the second is a loss. Include 500 tasks in the plan and charge, say, $0.08 for each extra task, and the heavy user pays for what they use.

Five steps

  1. Measure your real cost per task, including retries and long inputs.
  2. Decide what is included in each tier so AI feels part of the product.
  3. Set an allowance that covers most customers and meter the rest.
  4. Show usage inside the app so overages never surprise anyone.
  5. Review prices every quarter, because model costs and customer habits change fast.

Which AI SaaS pricing model should you choose?

There is no single best AI pricing model. Choose the unit that customers can understand and that tracks your cost driver closely enough to protect the business. A product that summarizes one short email has a different cost profile from an agent that searches documents, calls tools and runs several model steps.

ModelWorks well whenMain risk
Per seatUsage is light and similar across users, or AI is a supporting feature.A few power users can consume far more resources than the average seat.
Usage-basedCustomers can connect usage directly to value, such as API calls or documents processed.Unpredictable bills can make buyers hesitant.
CreditsDifferent actions have different costs and customers need a visible allowance.Opaque credit conversion can frustrate customers if the unit is hard to understand.
HybridYou want a predictable subscription plus a usage allowance and paid overages.Allowance size and overage rules need careful design.
Outcome-basedThe result can be measured and attributed reliably, such as a verified workflow completed.Disputes arise when success criteria or attribution are unclear.

For many early products, a hybrid structure is a sensible starting hypothesis, not a universal industry rule. It gives customers a known base price while letting the business meter unusually heavy usage. Validate it with customer interviews and actual cost data.

Calculate gross margin before setting the allowance

Start with the full variable cost of one successful task. Include model calls, retrieval or search, third-party tools, storage or compute that scales with usage, retries and human review where it is part of normal delivery. Our guide to calculating AI API costs explains how to measure the model portion.

For a simple illustration, assume a plan costs $30 per month, includes 500 completed AI tasks, and each task costs $0.04 in variable AI charges. The included usage costs $20, leaving $10 before payment fees, support, hosting, sales and other operating costs. This is not a 33% company gross margin calculation because it excludes those other costs.

If the customer completes 5,000 tasks, the extra 4,500 tasks cost $180 at the same assumed unit cost. If overage is $0.08 per task, the customer pays another $360 and the total plan revenue is $390. Against $200 of assumed AI cost, $190 remains before all other costs. This shows why the included allowance and overage price must be tested together.

Test the economics of an AI feature plan

Change these assumptions to estimate monthly revenue and variable task cost for one customer. The estimate excludes payment fees, support, fixed hosting and other operating expenses.

AI plan unit-economics calculator

Estimated revenue: $30.00
Variable task cost: $20.00
Contribution before other costs: $10.00

This is a planning estimate, not a recommended market price. Use measured cost per successful task and test customer willingness to pay.

How to choose an allowance

  1. Measure a real usage distribution. Use several weeks of representative product data if you have it. Look at median usage and heavy-use percentiles, not only the average.
  2. Segment customers by job. A support team, a solo founder and an agency may use the same feature very differently.
  3. Set an allowance around a customer outcome. “500 document summaries” is easier to understand than an unexplained bucket of 40,000 tokens.
  4. Model the high-usage case. Check whether a customer who uses the full allowance plus overages remains commercially viable.
  5. Revisit the unit when the product changes. A new agent workflow or longer context window can change cost per task.

Make AI usage understandable inside the product

Show customers what counts as a task, how much of their allowance remains, when it resets and what happens after they reach the limit. Send a warning before an overage begins. Offer a way to set a spend cap or pause optional AI work where practical. If you use credits, publish a simple conversion table and explain whether failed tasks consume credits.

Do not quietly change the value of a credit or the definition of a completed task. Pricing is part of the product experience. Confusing billing can erase the trust created by a useful AI feature.

Test the price with customer evidence

Ask potential buyers how they budget for the problem today, what outcome would justify paying more, and whether they prefer a predictable monthly allowance or a bill tied to usage. Test a few clear packages rather than asking “what would you pay?” in the abstract. Compare conversion, activation, usage, expansion, churn and support tickets after launch.

Track contribution margin by customer cohort. If the most engaged customers are also the least profitable, you may have a pricing or product-efficiency problem. If customers rarely reach the allowance, the package may be too generous or the feature may not be valuable enough to drive usage.

Common AI pricing mistakes

  • Pricing from model token rates alone: model fees are only one part of delivering a reliable feature.
  • Calling usage unlimited: this creates open-ended exposure when a workflow can loop or be automated.
  • Charging for tokens customers cannot interpret: expose a meaningful product unit where possible.
  • Ignoring quality: the cheapest model may create more retries, corrections or support costs.
  • Changing limits without warning: explain plan changes and give customers time to adapt.

Frequently asked questions

Should AI features be priced per user or per usage?

Use per-seat pricing when usage is relatively predictable and the feature is included in the value of the seat. Use usage pricing when cost or customer value rises directly with activity. A hybrid model can combine a base subscription with an included allowance and transparent overages.

How much should I charge for an AI feature?

There is no reliable universal price. Calculate cost per successful task, understand how much customers value the outcome, then test a price that covers variable costs and contributes to the rest of the business. Validate with real usage and willingness-to-pay evidence.

Are AI credits better than tokens?

Credits can make billing easier when different AI actions have different costs. Tokens are more transparent to technical buyers but can be difficult for non-technical customers to predict. If you use credits, explain exactly how each action consumes them.

Can I offer unlimited AI usage?

Only if you have evidence that the cost distribution is predictable and the plan remains profitable under heavy use. Otherwise, set a fair-use policy, allowance, usage cap or overage structure that customers can understand.
